title: Canadian Space Agency: monitoring radiation and why we do science in space

pages.title: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
pages.challenge_note: How the CSA monitors space radiation to protect astronaut health on long-duration missions, including Canadian technologies used to measure exposure.

pages.title: Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?
pages.challenge_note: How the space environment enables experiments that cannot be done on Earth, and how ISS research advances human health and technology.

radiation_facts.text: Neutron radiation makes up about 30% of the total radiation on the International Space Station.
ISS astronauts typically receive about 150 microsieverts of neutron radiation a day, hundreds of times more than on Earth.
Neutron doses are generally lower in the sleeping quarters than elsewhere on the station, and differ only slightly between the seven US modules.
Long-term neutron exposure can potentially cause cataracts, bone-marrow damage and cancer.
On spacewalks, measured doses to the skin, eyes and blood-forming organs were about 6, 13 and 25 times the internationally set limits for nuclear-industry workers.

instruments.name: MOSFET dosimeters
instruments.what: Miniature silicon dosimeters: radiation shifts the sensor's voltage. Shields of different thickness estimate dose to the skin, eyes and blood-forming organs.

instruments.name: EVARM
instruments.what: Three MOSFET badges worn inside the spacesuit (one on the lower leg, two on the torso) measured organ doses during spacewalks.

instruments.name: Radi-N and Radi-N2 bubble detectors
instruments.what: Finger-sized gel tubes: a neutron that hits a droplet leaves a visible bubble to count. Eight per session for a week: six around the station, one worn by the astronaut, one in the sleeping quarters.

instruments.name: Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS)
instruments.what: A compact instrument that measures neutron exposure continuously and autonomously; the CSA awarded a $5.5 million contract to keep developing it.

body_effects.text: Bone marrow makes fewer red blood cells, which can lead to anaemia; fewer white cells raise infection risk and sensitivity to radiation.
Astronauts can become disoriented and misjudge the direction and speed of their movement; some get space sickness.
Blood vessels stiffen and age faster, and insulin resistance can develop, which may lead to type 2 diabetes.
Muscles lose mass and strength, reflexes slow, and exercise is less effective.
Adults over 50 lose about 1% of bone mass a year; astronauts can lose up to 1.5% a month.

earth_benefits: Weightlessness causes changes that resemble accelerated ageing and a sedentary lifestyle.
Six months in orbit gives data that would take years to gather on Earth.
Findings may help people with balance problems, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disorders and type 2 diabetes.
About 200 international experiments are on board the ISS at any time.
